title: Divus Iulius
titleEn: Caesar's Star, and the Poet's Last Word — Metamorphoses XV.745–879
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Rome's newest god is no incomer. Ovid turns from Aesculapius to Caesar and argues that Caesar's greatest achievement was not Britain, nor the Nile, nor his triumphs, but his son — so Caesar must be made a god to make Augustus a god's child. Venus, seeing the conspiracy take shape, runs through heaven begging the gods to stop it; they cannot break the Fates' decrees, and answer with portents instead: weapons clashing in black cloud, a sallow sun, weeping ivory, a severed lobe in the entrails. The swords go into the senate house anyway. Jupiter shows Venus the iron archive of destiny and reads out what stands written there — Mutina, Pharsalia, Philippi, the Egyptian queen, the peace, the laws, the succession — then tells her to carry her Caesar's soul into the sky, where it becomes a comet. The poem ends with a prayer that Augustus's own ascent come late, and with Ovid's claim on his own survival.

sentences.t:
Hic tamen accessit delubris advena nostris:
Caesar in urbe sua deus est;
sentences.l: He, however, came to our shrines as a newcomer: Caesar is a god in his own city;
sentences.i: He, though, came to our shrines a stranger: Caesar is a god in his own city;
sentences.n: The contrast opens the poem's last movement. “Hic” points back to Aesculapius, brought to Rome from Epidaurus in the lines just before this part, who arrives an “advena”, an incomer; Caesar is a god at home, in a city that is already his. “delubris … nostris” is dative with “accessit”, “came to our shrines”.

sentences.t:
quem Marte togaque
praecipuum non bella magis finita triumphis
resque domi gestae properataque gloria rerum
in sidus vertere novum stellamque comantem,
quam sua progenies;
sentences.l: and him, preeminent in war and in the toga, his wars finished with triumphs and his deeds done at home and the hurried glory of his exploits did not turn into a new star and a comet more than his own offspring did;
sentences.i: and it was not his wars ended in triumphs, nor what he did at home, nor the glory of his deeds heaped up in haste, that turned him — supreme in war and in peace alike — into a new star, a comet: it was his own son;
sentences.n: “vertere” is the poetic third-plural perfect for “verterunt”, the -ēre ending you will meet constantly in this poem. “Marte togaque” is metonymy: Mars for war, the toga for civil life at Rome. The comparison is “non magis … quam”, “not more … than”, so the whole weight falls on the last item, “sua progenies” — Augustus, Caesar's son by adoption. “stellam comantem”, a “haired star”, is the Latin for a comet: the one seen at Caesar's funeral games, which returns at line 849.

sentences.t:
neque enim de Caesaris actis
ullum maius opus, quam quod pater exstitit huius:
sentences.l: for of Caesar's deeds there is no greater work than that he stood forth as this man's father:
sentences.i: for among everything Caesar did there is no greater achievement than this — that he proved to be the father of this man:
sentences.n: Verbless: supply “est”. “huius”, “of this man”, points at Augustus without naming him, and the whole argument down to line 760 keeps him unnamed: the name does not arrive until line 860. “exstitit” is from “existere”, to step forth, to prove to be; Magnus prints the “exst-” spelling, where other texts print “extitit”.

sentences.t:
scilicet aequoreos plus est domuisse Britannos
perque papyriferi septemflua flumina Nili
victrices egisse rates
sentences.l: no doubt it is more to have tamed the sea-girt Britons, and to have driven victorious ships through the seven-flowing streams of papyrus-bearing Nile,
sentences.i: Doubtless it was more to have tamed the sea-ringed Britons, to have driven victorious ships up the seven-mouthed streams of the papyrus-bearing Nile,
sentences.n: “scilicet” is ironic here — “of course”, “no doubt” — setting up a rhetorical question that does not close until line 758. The perfect infinitives (“domuisse”, “egisse”, and “adiecisse” and “meruisse” to come) are all subjects of “est”: it is more to have done these things than to have fathered such a man. “septemflua” and “papyriferi” are compound adjectives of the kind Ovid coins freely; the seven streams are the mouths of the Nile delta.

sentences.t:
Numidasque rebelles
Cinyphiumque Iubam Mithridateisque tumentem
nominibus Pontum populo adiecisse Quirini
sentences.l: and to have added the rebellious Numidians and Cinyphian Juba and Pontus swelling with Mithridatic names to the people of Quirinus,
sentences.i: to have added to the people of Quirinus the rebel Numidians, Juba of the Cinyps, and Pontus swollen with the name of Mithridates,
sentences.n: Quirinus is the deified Romulus, so “populus Quirini” is simply the Roman people. Juba I of Numidia fought Caesar in Africa; the Cinyps is a river in Libya, standing here for the whole region. “Mithridateis … nominibus” is a plural for the dynasty of that name in Pontus, and an ablative of cause with “tumentem”, “swelling with” — puffed up by.

sentences.t:
et multos meruisse, aliquos egisse triumphos,
quam tantum genuisse virum?
sentences.l: and to have earned many triumphs, to have celebrated some, than to have fathered so great a man?
sentences.i: to have earned many triumphs and actually celebrated a few — more than to have fathered so great a man?
sentences.n: “egisse triumphos” is the technical phrase for holding a triumph, the procession up to the Capitol; the point of “multos meruisse, aliquos egisse” is that Caesar earned more of them than he was granted. The “quam” here at last answers the “plus” of line 752, six lines back.

sentences.t:
Quo praeside rerum
humano generi, superi, favistis abunde!
sentences.l: With him as guardian of the world, gods above, you have favoured the human race abundantly!
sentences.i: In giving the world such a guardian, gods above, you favoured the human race beyond measure.
sentences.n: “Quo praeside” is an ablative absolute made of two nouns with no participle at all — a shape Latin allows and English cannot copy: “with him as protector”. “rerum”, literally “of things”, is the ordinary Roman phrase for the world or the state. The direct address to the gods (“superi”) is an apostrophe, Ovid turning aside from the narrative to speak to them — he will do it again at length from line 861.

sentences.t:
Ne foret hic igitur mortali semine cretus,
ille deus faciendus erat.
sentences.l: Therefore, so that this man should not be sprung from mortal seed, that one had to be made a god.
sentences.i: So, in order that this man should not be born of mortal stock, the other had to be made a god.
sentences.n: The logic runs deliberately backwards: Caesar is deified so that Augustus can be the son of a god. “cretus” is the perfect participle of “cresco” used in the sense “sprung from, born of”, with the ablative “mortali semine”. “foret” is an old alternative form for “esset”. “hic” is Augustus and “ille” Caesar — the near one and the far one, as usual in Latin.

sentences.t:
Quod ut aurea vidit
Aeneae genetrix, vidit quoque triste parari
pontifici letum et coniurata arma moveri,
sentences.l: When golden Aeneas's mother saw this, and saw also that a grim death was being prepared for the pontifex and that sworn weapons were being set in motion,
sentences.i: When the golden mother of Aeneas saw this, and saw too that a grim death was being readied for the pontifex and that conspiring blades were on the move,
sentences.n: “Quod” is a connecting relative — “and this” — picking up the whole preceding thought; a sentence opening with “quod”, “quae”, “quem” usually means “and this”, “and she”, “and him”. The golden mother of Aeneas is Venus, ancestress of the Julian line. “pontifici” is dative: Caesar was pontifex maximus, and the title makes his murder a sacrilege, which is the argument Venus will press. “coniurata arma” transfers the conspirators' oath from the men to their weapons.

sentences.t:
palluit et cunctis, ut cuique erat obvia, divis
“adspice” dicebat,
sentences.l: she went pale, and to all the gods, as she came upon each one, kept saying “look,
sentences.i: she went white, and to every god, as she met them one by one, kept saying, “Look —
sentences.n: “dicebat” is imperfect, and the tense is the point: not one speech but the same words over and over, to each god in turn. “ut cuique erat obvia”, literally “as she was in the way of each”, is the ordinary idiom for meeting someone. “adspice” keeps Magnus's spelling, where other texts print “aspice”.

sentences.t:
“quanta mihi mole parentur
insidiae quantaque caput cum fraude petatur,
quod de Dardanio solum mihi restat Iulo.
sentences.l: with what great effort a plot is being prepared against me, and with what great treachery that head is being hunted which alone is left to me from Dardanian Iulus.
sentences.i: see with what machinery this plot is being built against me, with what treachery they hunt the one head left to me out of Dardanian Iulus's line.
sentences.n: Both “quanta … mole” and “quanta … cum fraude” are indirect questions depending on “adspice”, which is why their verbs are subjunctive (“parentur”, “petatur”). “mihi” is a dative of disadvantage — the plot is aimed at Venus herself, not only at Caesar. Iulus is Aeneas's son, from whom the Julian family claimed its descent; “Dardanio” means Trojan, from Dardanus, founder of the Trojan line.

sentences.t:
Solane semper ero iustis exercita curis,
quam modo Tydidae Calydonia vulneret hasta,
nunc male defensae confundant moenia Troiae,
sentences.l: Shall I alone always be harried by just cares — I whom just now the Calydonian spear of Tydeus's son wounds, whom now the walls of badly defended Troy confound,
sentences.i: Am I alone always to be harried by griefs I have every right to — I whom the Calydonian spear of Tydeus's son wounds one moment, whom the walls of Troy, so poorly defended, undo the next,
sentences.n: The relative clauses take present subjunctives (“vulneret”, “confundant”, then “videam” in the next lines) — a causal or characterising relative: “since it is I who…”. Diomedes, son of Tydeus and king of Argos, wounded Venus in the hand at Troy; the spear is called Calydonian because his father's house came from Calydon, and she is still counting the wound. “modo … nunc”, just now and now, keeps centuries-old injuries fresh, so that the wound and the fall of Troy arrive as if they were this morning's.

sentences.t:
quae videam natum longis erroribus actum
iactarique freto sedesque intrare silentum
bellaque cum Turno gerere,
sentences.l: I who must see my son driven by long wanderings and tossed on the sea and entering the abodes of the silent and waging wars with Turnus,
sentences.i: I who must watch my son driven through long wanderings, flung about on the sea, going down into the dwellings of the silent, fighting his wars with Turnus —
sentences.n: “natum” is Aeneas. Four infinitives hang on “videam”: “actum” (supply “esse”), “iactari”, “intrare”, “gerere”. The “seats of the silent ones” are the underworld, which Aeneas enters in the Aeneid; Turnus is the Rutulian king who fights him for Latium in the second half of that poem.

sentences.t:
aut, si vera fatemur,
cum Iunone magis? Quid nunc antiqua recordor
damna mei generis?
sentences.l: or, if we confess the truth, with Juno rather? Why do I now recall the ancient losses of my line?
sentences.i: or rather, if we are being honest, with Juno? Why am I calling up the old losses of my line now?
sentences.n: The correction is grim: Turnus was only Juno's instrument, so the real war was with Juno. “fatemur” is first person plural — Venus folding her divine audience into the admission. “damna mei generis”, the losses of her family, sums up the whole Trojan and Julian catalogue she has just run through.

sentences.t:
Timor hic meminisse priorum
non sinit: en acui sceleratos cernitis enses?
sentences.l: This fear does not allow me to remember earlier things: look, do you see wicked swords being sharpened?
sentences.i: This fear leaves no room for remembering what came before: look — do you see the criminal blades being whetted?
sentences.n: “meminisse priorum” takes a genitive, as “memini” regularly does: to be mindful of earlier things. “acui” is the present passive infinitive of “acuo”, standing in indirect statement after “cernitis” — “you see [that] swords are being sharpened”. “sceleratos” shifts the guilt from the assassins onto the weapons, exactly as “coniurata arma” did at line 763.

sentences.t:
Quos prohibete, precor, facinusque repellite, neve
caede sacerdotis flammas exstinguite Vestae!”
sentences.l: And these hold back, I beg, and drive off the crime, and do not put out Vesta's flames with the slaughter of her priest!”
sentences.i: Hold them off, I beg you, beat back the crime — do not quench Vesta's fire with the murder of her own priest!”
sentences.n: “Quos” is another connecting relative, “and these”, picking up the swords of the previous line. “neve … exstinguite” is a poetic negative command using the plain imperative where prose would say “nolite exstinguere”. The argument turns once more on Caesar's office: as pontifex maximus he had charge of Vesta's cult, so his murder would be the putting-out of the fire that guarantees Rome. Venus is asking the gods to save the city, not merely her descendant.

sentences.t:
Talia nequiquam toto Venus anxia caelo
verba iacit superosque movet,
sentences.l: Such words anxious Venus flings in vain through all heaven, and she stirs the gods above,
sentences.i: Such words anxious Venus flings through the whole of heaven, and to no purpose; she does move the gods above,
sentences.n: “nequiquam”, “in vain”, lands in the second word of the sentence, before we are told what happens: the outcome is given away ahead of the appeal. “toto … caelo” is a bare ablative of place with no preposition, which verse allows freely.

sentences.t:
qui rumpere quamquam
ferrea non possunt veterum decreta sororum,
signa tamen luctus dant haud incerta futuri.
sentences.l: who, although they cannot break the iron decrees of the ancient sisters, nevertheless give signs, and not uncertain ones, of the grief to come.
sentences.i: and though they cannot break the iron decrees of the ancient sisters, they do give signs — unmistakable ones — of the grief to come.
sentences.n: The “ancient sisters” are the three Fates, and their decrees are “ferrea”, iron — an image the passage will pick up again when Jupiter shows Venus an archive of bronze and iron at line 810. “haud incerta” is litotes, “not uncertain” standing for “perfectly plain”, a favourite Latin understatement.

sentences.l: Arms clattering among black clouds, they say, and terrible trumpets and horns heard in the sky gave warning beforehand of the abomination;
sentences.i: Weapons, they say, clashed in the black clouds; there were terrible trumpets, and horns heard in the sky, all of them warning of the abomination to come;
sentences.n: “ferunt”, “they say”, throws the first portent into indirect statement: arma … praemonuisse, weapons to have given warning. The catalogue moves in and out of that reported frame over the next fifteen lines — plain indicatives in between — and “ferunt” returns at line 798 to close it, so the whole run of prodigies is at one remove, reported rather than vouched for. “nefas” is not merely a crime but a thing contrary to divine law, unspeakable. “crepitantia” is the clattering of metal on metal.

sentences.t:
solis quoque tristis imago
lurida sollicitis praebebat lumina terris.
sentences.l: the sun's grim image too offered sallow light to anxious lands.
sentences.i: the sun's own disc too, gone grim, offered a sickly light to a frightened world.
sentences.n: “quoque” here is the adverb “also” — but watch it in this poem, because the same spelling can be “quō-que”, “and by which”, and only the sense separates them. “imago solis” is the visible disc; “lurida” is the yellowish pallor of sickness; and “sollicitis … terris” is a transferred epithet, since it is not the lands that are anxious but the people on them.

sentences.t:
Saepe faces visae mediis ardere sub astris,
saepe inter nimbos guttae cecidere cruentae.
sentences.l: Often torches were seen to burn beneath the midst of the stars, often among the rainclouds bloody drops fell.
sentences.i: Again and again torches were seen burning below the stars; again and again drops of blood came down with the rain.
sentences.n: “faces”, torches, are the fire-brands of meteors, a standard prodigy in Roman reports. “visae” needs “sunt” supplied. “cecidere” is once more the poetic third-plural perfect for “ceciderunt”. Both lines begin with “saepe”, and the anaphora is what gives the catalogue its relentlessness.

sentences.t:
Caerulus et vultum ferrugine Lucifer atra
sparsus erat, sparsi Lunares sanguine currus.
sentences.l: And Lucifer was dark-blue and sprinkled as to his face with black iron-rust; the chariots of the Moon were sprinkled with blood.
sentences.i: The Morning Star was blue-dark, his face spattered with a black metallic stain; the Moon's chariot was spattered with blood.
sentences.n: “vultum” is a Greek accusative of respect after the passive participle “sparsus” — “sprinkled as to his face” — a construction Ovid reaches for whenever something is worn, stained or bound. Lucifer, the morning star, is the planet Venus, so the stain falls on the goddess's own star, which sharpens the omen against her. “Lunares … currus” is a poetic plural for one chariot, and the second “sparsi” needs “sunt” supplied.

sentences.t:
Tristia mille locis Stygius dedit omina bubo,
mille locis lacrimavit ebur, cantusque feruntur
auditi sanctis et verba minantia lucis.
sentences.l: In a thousand places the Stygian owl gave grim omens, in a thousand places ivory wept, and songs are reported to have been heard in the holy groves, and threatening words.
sentences.i: In a thousand places the owl of the Styx gave its grim omens, in a thousand places ivory wept, and singing was heard, they say, in the sacred groves, and words that threatened.
sentences.n: The “bubo” is the eagle-owl, called Stygian because its cry belongs to the underworld. Weeping cult statues — the ivory is the inlay of an image — are a recurring prodigy in Roman records. “lucis” here is from “lucus”, a grove, not from “lux”, light: the singing was heard in the sacred groves. “feruntur auditi” keeps the reporting construction going, this time personally: they are said to have been heard.

sentences.t:
Victima nulla litat magnosque instare tumultus
fibra monet, caesumque caput reperitur in extis.
sentences.l: No victim gives a favourable sign, and the fibre warns that great upheavals are at hand, and a severed head is found among the entrails.
sentences.i: No sacrifice comes out favourable; the liver warns that great upheavals are at hand, and in the entrails a severed lobe is found.
sentences.n: “litat” is the technical verb of Roman sacrifice: not to offer, but to obtain a favourable sign from what is offered. “fibra” is the lobe of the liver that the haruspex reads, and “caput” is the technical name for its projecting lobe, whose absence or severing was the worst omen the discipline knew — Roman tradition reported exactly such a defect at Caesar's last sacrifice. The verbs here are all present (“litat”, “monet”, “reperitur”), the historic present pulling the reader into the moment after a run of perfects.

sentences.t:
Inque foro circumque domos et templa deorum
nocturnos ululasse canes umbrasque silentum
erravisse ferunt motamque tremoribus urbem.
sentences.l: And in the forum and around the houses and the temples of the gods dogs howled by night, they say, and the shades of the silent wandered, and the city was shaken by tremors.
sentences.i: In the forum, around the houses and the temples of the gods, dogs howled in the night — so they say — and the shades of the dead walked, and the city was shaken with tremors.
sentences.n: “ferunt” again, with three accusative-and-infinitive clauses hanging on it: dogs to have howled, shades to have wandered, and the city to have been shaken (“motam”, with “esse” left out). “nocturnos” is an adjective doing an adverb's work, “by night”, which Latin much prefers. The “shades of the silent ones” are the same dead whose dwellings Aeneas entered at line 772.

sentences.t:
Non tamen insidias venturaque vincere fata
praemonitus potuere deum,
sentences.l: Yet the forewarnings of the gods could not overcome the ambush and the fates that were coming,
sentences.i: Yet the gods' warnings could not defeat the plot, or the fate on its way;
sentences.n: “praemonitus” is not the participle it looks like but a fourth-declension noun in the nominative plural, “forewarnings”, and it is the subject of “potuere”. “deum” is the old genitive plural for “deorum”, common in verse. “potuere” is another poetic third-plural perfect. Sixteen lines of portents are cancelled in a line and a half.

sentences.t:
strictique feruntur
in templum gladii; neque enim locus ullus in urbe
ad facinus diramque placet nisi curia, caedem.
sentences.l: and drawn swords are carried into the temple; for no place in the city pleases for the crime and the dreadful slaughter except the senate house.
sentences.i: and drawn swords are carried into the temple; for no place in the city suits the crime and that dreadful killing but the senate house.
sentences.n: The word order of line 802 is violently split: “ad facinus diramque … caedem” wraps right around “placet nisi curia”, so that “caedem”, slaughter, falls last in the line and last in the sentence, with the comma before it in Magnus's text. “templum” and “curia” are the same building — the senate was meeting in the Curia attached to Pompey's theatre — and calling it a temple is what makes the sacrilege.

sentences.t:
Tum vero Cytherea manu percussit utraque
pectus et Aeneaden molitur condere nube,
sentences.l: Then indeed the Cytherean struck her breast with each hand and works to hide the descendant of Aeneas in a cloud,
sentences.i: Then indeed the Cytherean beat her breast with both hands and set about hiding Aeneas's descendant in a cloud,
sentences.n: “Cytherea” is Venus, named from Cythera, the island off which she rose from the sea. “Aeneaden” is a Greek accusative singular of the patronymic “Aeneades”, a descendant of Aeneas — here Caesar, who is separated from Aeneas by the whole Julian line. The tense shifts from perfect (“percussit”) to present (“molitur”) inside the sentence, the historic present quickening the action just as the blow lands.

sentences.t:
qua prius infesto Paris est ereptus Atridae
et Diomedeos Aeneas fugerat enses.
sentences.l: in which formerly Paris was snatched away from the hostile son of Atreus, and Aeneas had escaped the swords of Diomedes.
sentences.i: the same cloud in which Paris was once snatched from the son of Atreus in his fury, and Aeneas had fled the swords of Diomedes.
sentences.n: Two rescues out of the Iliad: Aphrodite hides Paris from Menelaus, and Apollo hides Aeneas from Diomedes. “Atridae” is a dative of separation with “ereptus”, snatched from. “Diomedeos … enses” turns a name into an adjective, “Diomedean swords”, where English wants a genitive. The point of recalling both is that this time the rescue will not be permitted.

sentences.t:
Talibus hanc genitor: “Sola insuperabile fatum,
nata, movere paras?
sentences.l: Her father to her with such words: “Alone, daughter, are you preparing to move an unconquerable fate?
sentences.i: Her father answered her so: “Are you alone, daughter, preparing to shift an unconquerable fate?
sentences.n: “Talibus hanc genitor” has no verb at all — supply something like “adloquitur”, “addresses her”. The ellipsis is a mannerism of epic speech-introductions and Ovid uses it for speed. “genitor” is Jupiter. “Sola” stands first in the speech for its emphasis: alone of all the gods, and against all of them.

sentences.t:
Intres licet ipsa sororum
tecta trium: cernes illic molimine vasto
ex aere et solido rerum tabularia ferro,
sentences.l: You may enter the dwellings of the three sisters yourself: you will see there, of vast construction, the record-office of the world, made of bronze and solid iron,
sentences.i: Go in yourself, if you like, to the house of the three sisters: there you will see, built on a vast scale, the world's record-office in bronze and solid iron,
sentences.n: “licet” with the subjunctive “intres” is permissive: “you are free to enter”. The three sisters are the Fates again. “tabularia” is the Roman state archive — the Tabularium stood on the Capitol, holding the records of the city — so Ovid gives destiny the furniture of a records office — except that these tablets are cast in bronze and solid iron rather than written on wax or wood, and cannot be amended.

sentences.t:
quae neque concussum caeli neque fulminis iram
nec metuunt ullas tuta atque aeterna ruinas.
sentences.l: which fear neither a shaking of the sky nor the anger of the lightning nor any collapses at all, being safe and everlasting.
sentences.i: and they fear neither the shock of the sky nor the wrath of the lightning nor any ruin at all: safe, and everlasting.
sentences.n: “concussum” is a fourth-declension verbal noun in the accusative, “a shaking”; Magnus prints it, while some editions read “concursum”, “a colliding”, which would have the heavens crash together rather than shudder. “tuta atque aeterna” are nominative plural neuter agreeing with “tabularia”, and stand where English wants a clause: because they are safe and eternal.

sentences.t:
Invenies illic incisa adamante perenni
fata tui generis: legi ipse animoque notavi
et referam, ne sis etiamnum ignara futuri.
sentences.l: You will find there the fates of your line, cut into everlasting adamant: I have read them myself and marked them in my mind, and I will report them, so that you may not still be ignorant of the future.
sentences.i: There you will find the fates of your line cut into everlasting adamant. I have read them myself and fixed them in my mind, and I will tell you, so that you need not be in the dark about the future any longer.
sentences.n: “adamas” is the hardest imaginable substance, steel or an unbreakable stone; the ablative “adamante” is one of means — the letters cut with it, or into it. “ignara futuri” takes a genitive: not knowing of what is to come. Jupiter's claim to have read the tablets himself is what makes the prophecy that follows unanswerable.

sentences.t:
Hic sua complevit, pro quo, Cytherea, laboras,
tempora, perfectis, quos terrae debuit, annis.
sentences.l: This man, for whom you are labouring, Cytherea, has filled out his own span, the years which he owed to the earth having been completed.
sentences.i: The man you are labouring for, Cytherea, has filled out his span; the years he owed the earth are done.
sentences.n: The word order is the whole effect: “sua … tempora”, his own time, is prised apart by the interjection “pro quo, Cytherea, laboras”, so that the reader waits until the next line for the noun. “perfectis … annis” is an ablative absolute with a relative clause tucked inside it. And “debuit” turns a life into a loan: what was owed has been paid, and the account is closed.

sentences.t:
Ut deus accedat caelo templisque colatur,
tu facies natusque suus,
sentences.l: That he may come to heaven as a god and be worshipped in temples, you will bring about, you and his own son,
sentences.i: That he should come to heaven a god and be worshipped in temples — you will see to that, you and his own son,
sentences.n: “Ut … accedat … colatur” is a substantive clause serving as the object of “facies”: you will make it happen that… “caelo” is dative with “accedat”, come to heaven. “natus suus” is Augustus, adopted in Caesar's will, and “suus” insists on precisely the relationship this whole passage exists to establish.

sentences.t:
qui nominis heres
impositum feret unus onus caesique parentis
nos in bella suos fortissimus ultor habebit.
sentences.l: who, heir of the name, will bear alone the burden laid upon him, and, bravest avenger of his slaughtered father, will have us as his own in his wars.
sentences.i: who, heir to the name, will carry the burden laid on him alone, and, bravest of avengers for a murdered father, will have us on his side in his wars.
sentences.n: “nominis heres” is legally exact: Augustus inherited the name Caesar by testament, and the burden along with it. “unus” is emphatic — alone, without a colleague. “caesi parentis” is an objective genitive with “ultor”, the avenger of the murdered father, not by him. The boldest phrase is “nos … suos”, the gods themselves enrolled as his followers.

sentences.t:
Illius auspiciis obsessae moenia pacem
victa petent Mutinae, Pharsalia sentiet illum.
Emathiique iterum madefient caede Philippi,
sentences.l: Under his auspices the walls of besieged Mutina, conquered, will sue for peace; Pharsalia will feel him. And Emathian Philippi will again be soaked with slaughter,
sentences.i: Under his auspices the walls of besieged Mutina will be beaten and sue for peace; Pharsalia will feel his hand; Emathian Philippi will be drenched a second time in slaughter,
sentences.n: “auspiciis” is technical: a Roman commander fought under his own auspices, the right to take the omens before battle, so the word assigns him credit and authority at once. Mutina (Modena) was besieged in 43 BC; Pharsalia in Thessaly is where Caesar beat Pompey in 48; Philippi in Macedonia is where Antony and Octavian beat the assassins in 42. “Emathius” means Macedonian, and “iterum”, again, folds the two battlefields into one continuous Greek bloodletting, as Roman poets habitually do.

sentences.t:
et magnum Siculis nomen superabitur undis,
Romanique ducis coniunx Aegyptia taedae
non bene fisa cadet,
sentences.l: and a great name will be overcome in Sicilian waters, and the Egyptian wife of a Roman leader, having trusted not well in the marriage torch, will fall,
sentences.i: a great name will go down in Sicilian waters, and the Egyptian wife of a Roman commander, who trusted that marriage badly, will fall,
sentences.n: “magnum nomen” is a pun the Latin cannot help making: Sextus Pompeius, beaten at sea off Sicily in 36 BC, carried the name Magnus, “the Great”. Neither he nor the Egyptian queen is named — the prophecy keeps everyone at the level of title and epithet. “taedae” is dative with “fisa”, the perfect participle of the semi-deponent “fido”, which governs a dative; the wedding torch stands for the marriage by metonymy, and that marriage had no standing in Roman law.

sentences.t:
frustraque erit illa minata,
servitura suo Capitolia nostra Canopo.
sentences.l: and in vain will she have threatened that our Capitol would be slave to her own Canopus.
sentences.i: and her threat will have come to nothing — that our Capitol would serve her Canopus.
sentences.n: “minata” is from the deponent “minor”, to threaten, so “erit minata” is a future perfect with an active sense. “servitura … Capitolia” is a future participle in indirect statement with “esse” left out. Canopus, a town near Alexandria and a Roman byword for luxury, stands for Egypt; “nostra” set against “suo” puts the two capitals in one line, face to face. “Capitolia” is a poetic plural for the single hill.

sentences.t:
Quid tibi barbariem, gentesque ab utroque iacentes
oceano numerem?
sentences.l: Why should I count up for you the barbarian world, and the nations lying by either ocean?
sentences.i: Why should I number for you the barbarian lands, the nations lying along either ocean?
sentences.n: “numerem” is a deliberative subjunctive — “why am I to count?” — and “tibi” a dative of advantage, for your benefit. “barbariem” is an abstract noun for the barbarian world as a whole, not a plural of peoples. “ab utroque oceano” means from the eastern sea and the western: the ends of the earth.

sentences.t:
Quodcumque habitabile tellus
sustinet, huius erit: pontus quoque serviet illi!
sentences.l: Whatever habitable land the earth holds up will be his: the sea too will serve him!
sentences.i: Whatever habitable ground the earth carries will belong to him — and the sea will serve him too.
sentences.n: “huius erit” is a possessive genitive with the verb “to be”: will be of this man, will belong to him. Here “quoque” really is the adverb “also” — the caution from line 785 still stands, since the same letters can be “quō-que”, “and by which”.

sentences.t:
Pace data terris animum ad civilia vertet
iura suum legesque feret iustissimus auctor
exemploque suo mores reget
sentences.l: With peace given to the lands he will turn his mind to civil law, and will bring in laws, a most just author of them, and will govern conduct by his own example,
sentences.i: Once he has given the lands peace he will turn his mind to civil law, and will bring in laws, the most just of legislators, and will govern conduct by his own example,
sentences.n: “Pace data terris” is an ablative absolute — peace having been given to the lands — where English wants a clause with a conjunction; you meet this construction on nearly every page of the poem. “animum … suum” is split across a line-end by “ad civilia … iura”, which is itself split, and the tangle is Ovid showing what hexameter can do; the sense is simply that he will turn his own mind to civil law. “legesque feret” is the formal Roman phrase for proposing legislation, to carry a law.

sentences.t:
inque futuri
temporis aetatem venturorumque nepotum
prospiciens prolem sancta de coniuge natam
ferre simul nomenque suum curasque iubebit,
sentences.l: and, looking forward into the age of time to come and of grandchildren still to arrive, he will order the offspring born from his holy wife to bear at once both his name and his cares,
sentences.i: and, looking ahead into the age still to come and the descendants still to come, he will order the child born of his sacred wife to carry his name and his burdens together,
sentences.n: “prospiciens” governs the whole phrase “in … aetatem … nepotum”: he looks into the future as though into a country. “prolem … natam” is the accusative subject of “ferre” after “iubebit” — he will order the offspring to bear. Ovid describes the succession without naming the successor: the “holy wife” is Livia, and the child is her son by an earlier marriage, adopted as Augustus's heir. “simul” ties name and burden together in exactly the way “nominis heres … impositum … onus” did of Augustus himself at lines 819–820.

sentences.t:
nec nisi cum senior Pylios aequaverit annos,
aetherias sedes cognataque sidera tanget.
sentences.l: and not until, an old man, he has equalled the Pylian years will he touch the seats of the upper air and the stars of his kin.
sentences.i: and not until, grown old, he has matched the years of the Pylian will he touch the seats of the upper air and the stars he is kin to.
sentences.n: The Pylian years are Nestor's, king of Pylos and the Greek byword for extreme old age: the wish is that Augustus outlive three generations. “aequaverit” is a future perfect — the touching of heaven waits on the completing of the years. Magnus prints “Pylios”; some editions read “meritis”, which changes the sense to matching his years against his services rather than against Nestor's. “cognata sidera” takes the deification already for granted: up there the stars are relatives.

sentences.t:
Hanc animam interea caeso de corpore raptam
fac iubar, ut semper Capitolia nostra forumque
divus ab excelsa prospectet Iulius aede.”
sentences.l: Meanwhile make this soul, snatched from the slaughtered body, a light, so that the divine Julius may always look out over our Capitol and forum from his high temple.”
sentences.i: Meanwhile make this soul, once it is snatched from the murdered body, into a light, so that the deified Julius may look out for ever from his high temple over our Capitol and our forum.”
sentences.n: “fac” takes an accusative and a predicate accusative: make this soul into a light. “iubar” is a beam or radiance, here the comet. “divus Iulius” is the official title voted after the deification, and it is the heading Magnus gives this whole section; the high temple is the temple of Divus Iulius in the forum, whose statue did in fact look out over it — the mythology closing on a building the reader could walk past.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat, media cum sede senatus
constitit alma Venus, nulli cernenda,
sentences.l: Scarcely had he spoken these things, when in the middle of the senate's seat nourishing Venus took her stand, to be seen by no one,
sentences.i: He had scarcely spoken these things when kindly Venus took her stand in the middle of the senate house, visible to no one,
sentences.n: “Vix … cum” is the inverted “cum” construction, where the grammatically subordinate clause carries the real event; English does the same thing with “scarcely had he … when …”. “nulli cernenda” is a gerundive of possibility with a dative of agent: not to be seen by anyone. “alma”, nourishing, is one of Venus's standing cult epithets.

sentences.t:
suique
Caesaris eripuit membris neque in aera solvi
passa recentem animam caelestibus intulit astris.
sentences.l: and she snatched the soul of her own Caesar from his limbs, and, not having allowed it to be dissolved into the air, carried the fresh soul into the heavenly stars.
sentences.i: and she snatched her own Caesar's soul out of his limbs, and, not allowing it to dissolve into the air, carried the new-made soul up among the stars of heaven.
sentences.n: “membris” is an ablative of separation with “eripuit”. “passa” is the perfect participle of the deponent “patior” and is active in meaning — having allowed, not having been allowed — with the present passive infinitive “solvi” depending on it. “recentem animam”, the soul still fresh from the body, is why haste matters: left alone it would disperse into air. The murder itself is never described; Ovid cuts from the drawn swords straight to the soul.

sentences.t:
Dumque tulit, lumen capere atque ignescere sensit
emisitque sinu: luna volat altius illa,
flammiferumque trahens spatioso limite crinem
stella micat
sentences.l: And while she carried it, she felt it take light and catch fire, and released it from her breast: it flies higher than the moon, and, drawing a flame-bearing hair along a wide track, glitters as a star
sentences.i: And as she carried it she felt it take light and kindle, and let it go from her breast: it flies higher than the moon, and, trailing a fire-bearing hair down a broad path, glitters as a star
sentences.n: The subject changes without warning: Venus feels and releases, then “illa” — the soul — flies. “luna … altius illa” is an ablative of comparison, higher than the moon. “crinem” of a comet's tail is the same image as the “stella comans”, the haired star, at line 749, so the section is closing the figure it opened with; “limite” is the track it cuts across the sky.

sentences.t:
natique videns bene facta fatetur
esse suis maiora et vinci gaudet ab illo.
sentences.l: and, seeing the good deeds of his son, it acknowledges them to be greater than its own, and rejoices to be surpassed by him.
sentences.i: and, seeing his son's good deeds, it admits that they are greater than its own, and is glad to be outdone by him.
sentences.n: The star is Caesar and the son is Augustus; “nati” is Caesar's son, not Venus's, though the star is grammatically feminine and takes “it” or “she” in English. “bene facta”, printed as two words in the edition, means good deeds or benefactions. “suis maiora” is another ablative of comparison. The flattery is doing structural work: it lets Ovid finish the deification of the dead man by pointing at the living one, and it sets up the catalogue of sons outdoing fathers that follows.

sentences.t:
Hic sua praeferri quamquam vetat acta paternis,
libera fama tamen nullisque obnoxia iussis
invitum praefert unaque in parte repugnat:
sentences.l: Although this man forbids his own deeds to be preferred to his father's, free report nevertheless, and subject to no orders, prefers him against his will and in this one respect fights him:
sentences.i: Although he forbids his own deeds to be ranked above his father's, report — free, and answerable to no order — ranks him higher against his will, and in this one thing defies him:
sentences.n: “Hic” is Augustus, still unnamed until line 860. “praeferri” is a present passive infinitive after “vetat”, with “sua acta”, his own deeds, as its accusative subject and “paternis” a dative of the thing compared: to be put before his father's. “fama” here is public talk, what people say, rather than fame in the modern sense; calling it “libera” and “nullis obnoxia iussis” is a compliment and a joke at once, since very little else at Rome was. Magnus prints line 853; it is absent altogether from some texts.

sentences.t:
sic magni cedit titulis Agamemnonis Atreus,
Aegea sic Theseus, sic Pelea vicit Achilles;
sentences.l: so Atreus yields to the titles of great Agamemnon, so Theseus outdid Aegeus, so Achilles outdid Peleus;
sentences.i: so Atreus gives way to the titles of great Agamemnon, so Theseus surpassed Aegeus, so Achilles surpassed Peleus;
sentences.n: Three fathers outdone by their sons: Atreus and Agamemnon, Aegeus and Theseus, Peleus and Achilles. “titulis” means the honours inscribed on a monument, and so the public record of achievement. One “vicit” serves both halves of the second line. Magnus prints “magni”, attaching greatness to Agamemnon; some editions print “magnus”, which would make Atreus the great one giving way.

sentences.t:
denique, ut exemplis ipsos aequantibus utar,
sic et Saturnus minor est Iove:
sentences.l: finally, so that I may use examples matching the men themselves, so Saturn too is less than Jupiter:
sentences.i: and finally — to use comparisons on the same scale as the men themselves — so Saturn too is less than Jupiter:
sentences.n: “ut … utar” is a purpose clause with the deponent “utor”, which takes the ablative, hence “exemplis”. “aequantibus ipsos” means examples level with the subjects: Ovid apologising that mere heroes were too small a measure, and reaching for gods instead. “minor … Iove” is an ablative of comparison.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter arces
temperat aetherias et mundi regna triformis,
terra sub Augusto est; pater est et rector uterque.
sentences.l: Jupiter governs the heights of the upper air and the kingdoms of the threefold world; the earth is under Augustus; each is both father and ruler.
sentences.i: Jupiter rules the heights of heaven and the kingdoms of the threefold universe; the earth is under Augustus. Each of them is father and ruler both.
sentences.n: “mundi triformis” is the universe in three parts — sky, sea and underworld — shared out between Jupiter, Neptune and Pluto. The pairing is exact and audacious: Jupiter has the universe, Augustus the earth, and the balancing clause gives them the same two titles. The second of those titles is not decoration: Augustus had been voted “pater patriae”, father of his country, in 2 BC.

sentences.t:
Di, precor, Aeneae comites, quibus ensis et ignis
cesserunt,
sentences.l: Gods, I pray, companions of Aeneas, before whom sword and fire gave way,
sentences.i: Gods who went with Aeneas — I pray to you — before whom sword and fire gave way,
sentences.n: This begins a long chain of vocatives which runs to line 867 without ever reaching a main verb; the prayer itself does not arrive until line 868. The companions of Aeneas are the household gods he carried out of Troy, and “quibus ensis et ignis cesserunt” recalls that they came through the sack untouched, sword and fire making way for them. “precor” is dropped into the middle of the address, as the formula of a Roman prayer would be.

sentences.t:
dique Indigetes genitorque Quirine
urbis et invicti genitor Gradive Quirini,
Vestaque Caesareos inter sacrata penates,
et cum Caesarea tu, Phoebe domestice, Vesta,
sentences.l: and you native gods, and Quirinus, father of the city, and Gradivus, father of unconquered Quirinus, and Vesta, hallowed among Caesar's household gods, and you, Phoebus of the household, together with Caesarean Vesta,
sentences.i: and you gods of the soil, and Quirinus, father of the city, and Gradivus, father of unconquered Quirinus, and Vesta, made holy among Caesar's household gods, and you, Phoebus of the house, together with Caesar's Vesta,
sentences.n: Every name in the chain is deliberately domestic. The “di Indigetes” are Rome's own native deities; Quirinus is the deified Romulus, and Gradivus is a cult title of Mars, his father. Vesta and Phoebus are called Caesar's, and Phoebus “domesticus”, of the household, because both had moved onto the Palatine with Augustus: the temple of Apollo he built there adjoined his house, and when he became pontifex maximus in 12 BC he consecrated a shrine of Vesta inside the house itself. The state cult moved in with the emperor, which is exactly the fact Ovid is building the prayer on. The whole chain is stitched together with the enclitic “-que”, “and”.

sentences.t:
quique tenes altus Tarpeias Iuppiter arces,
quosque alios vati fas appellare piumque est:
sentences.l: and you, Jupiter, who hold on high the Tarpeian heights, and whatever others it is lawful and dutiful for a poet to call upon:
sentences.i: and you, Jupiter, holding the Tarpeian heights on high, and all the others a poet may lawfully and piously call on:
sentences.n: The Tarpeian heights are the Capitoline, where Jupiter Optimus Maximus had his temple; the Tarpeian rock is part of the same hill. “fas … piumque est” pairs divine law with religious duty, the two Roman words for what a man may properly do towards the gods. “vati”, dative with the impersonal “fas est”, is Ovid calling himself a “vates”, a prophet-poet rather than a mere maker — and he will use the word once more, in the very last line of the poem.

sentences.t:
tarda sit illa dies et nostro serior aevo,
qua caput Augustum, quem temperat, orbe relicto
accedat caelo faveatque precantibus absens!
sentences.l: let that day be slow, and later than our own lifetime, on which the head of Augustus, the world he governs having been left behind, may come to heaven and, absent, favour those who pray!
sentences.i: let that day come slowly, and later than our own lifetime, on which the person of Augustus, leaving behind the world he governs, comes to heaven and, absent, favours those who pray to him.
sentences.n: “sit”, and “accedat” and “faveat” after “qua”, are optative subjunctives: this is the wish the whole chain of vocatives has been climbing towards. “caput Augustum” is a reverential periphrasis, the person of Augustus. “orbe relicto” is an ablative absolute, and “quem temperat” has “orbem” for its antecedent — the same verb used of Jupiter ten lines earlier at 859. The prayer asks that his deification be postponed, so that the compliment and the loyalty are one sentence.

sentences.t:
Iamque opus exegi, quod nec Iovis ira nec ignis
nec poterit ferrum nec edax abolere vetustas.
sentences.l: And now I have finished a work which neither Jove's anger nor fire nor sword nor devouring age will be able to undo.
sentences.n: The epilogue begins. “exegi” is “I have driven through to the end”, the verb used of completing a task or a term of service, and it sets a made thing against the four powers that unmake things: divine anger, fire, iron and time. “edax vetustas”, devouring age, comes last and is the worst of them. Jupiter's anger heads the list eleven lines after line 860 set Jupiter and Augustus side by side as father and ruler.

sentences.t:
Cum volet, illa dies, quae nil nisi corporis huius
ius habet, incerti spatium mihi finiat aevi:
sentences.l: When it will, let that day, which has no right except over this body, end for me the span of an uncertain life:
sentences.i: Let that day, which holds rights over nothing but this body, end my uncertain span of life whenever it pleases:
sentences.n: “Cum volet”, when it shall wish, takes “dies” as its subject: the day of death is personified and given a will. “ius habet” with the genitive “corporis huius” is legal language — the day's jurisdiction reaches the body and stops there. “finiat” is a jussive subjunctive, a concession rather than a command: let it. “incerti … aevi” is uncertain in length and in outcome both, and it stands deliberately against “perennis”, everlasting, in the next line.

sentences.t:
parte tamen meliore mei super alta perennis
astra ferar, nomenque erit indelebile nostrum,
sentences.l: yet in the better part of me I shall be carried, everlasting, above the high stars, and my name will be indelible,
sentences.i: yet in the better part of me I shall be borne, undying, above the high stars, and my name will not be blotted out,
sentences.n: “parte meliore mei” is the soul, or the poem, or both — Ovid does not choose between them. “perennis” is nominative and agrees with the “I” of “ferar”, not with the stars: it is the poet who lasts through the years. “super alta astra” caps the whole book, which sent Caesar's soul among the stars twenty-nine lines earlier at 846; the poet now goes the same road as the god. “indelebile” means unable to be blotted out, and it is a word about writing.

sentences.t:
quaque patet domitis Romana potentia terris,
ore legar populi,
sentences.l: and wherever Roman power lies open over subdued lands, I shall be read on the mouth of the people,
sentences.i: and wherever Roman power extends over the lands it has subdued, I shall be read aloud on the people's lips,
sentences.n: “qua” is the relative adverb of place, where, with “-que” attached: and wherever. “domitis terris” is a bare ablative of place with “patet” — over the lands it has subdued; “domitis” is the participle of “domo”, tame, subdue, the same verb as “domuisse” back at line 752. “ore legar populi” means read aloud — Roman reading was normally out loud, so the poem survives as sound in a mouth rather than as marks on a page. Ovid measures his own reach by the empire's, which is homage and quiet one-upmanship in the same clause.

sentences.t:
perque omnia saecula fama,
siquid habent veri vatum praesagia, vivam.
sentences.l: and through all the ages in fame — if there is any truth in the foreseeing of poets, I shall live.
sentences.i: and through all the ages, in fame: and if what poets foresee holds any truth, I shall live on.
sentences.n: “fama” is ablative — in fame, by report — running parallel to “ore populi”. “vatum praesagia” brings back “vates” from line 867, the poet as prophet, so that the poem's last claim is a prophecy about its own author. In form “vivam” could be a wish, “may I live”, but the indicative “habent” in the condition makes it the future indicative: I shall live. It is the last word of the Metamorphoses.
